question: What are the rules on case management conferences?
answer:
## Commercial Court (rule/practice guide content)
- Only the specified parts of **Practice Direction 29** apply in the Commercial Court case management framework (subject to exclusions/modifications) [1][2].
- **Fixing the Case Management Conference**
  - If proceedings start by **Part 7 claim form**: the claimant must fix a date within **14 days** after all defendants who will file/serve a defence have done so (in co-operation with other parties) [4].
  - If proceedings start by **Part 8 claim form**: the claimant must fix a date within **14 days** after all defendants who wish to serve evidence have done so (in co-operation with other parties) [4].
  - If transferred to the Commercial Court: the claimant must apply within **14 days** of the transfer order date (unless the judge already held/gave directions for a CMC) [4].
- **If the claimant fails to apply**: any other party may apply for a Case Management Conference [5].
- **Importance and attendance**
  - The Commercial Court Guide describes the CMC as “very significant”, encouraging parties to agree directions, while still allowing attendance to be required [3].
  - If **all proposed directions are agreed**, the parties should file a **proposed Consent Order** as soon as possible, with an agreed covering letter explaining why attendance should not be required [3].
- **Hearing vs “on documents”**
  - Where **all proposed directions are not agreed**, there is a **general rule of an oral hearing** [3].
  - Exceptionally, an oral hearing may be dispensed with even if not all directions are agreed, if issues are straightforward and costs cannot be justified [3].
  - If CMC is sought **on documents**, the parties must provide the appropriate documents **by 12 noon on the Tuesday** of the week in which the CMC is fixed for the Friday; that timing is **strictly enforced** [3]. If documents aren’t provided in time, the CMC must be expected to go forward to an oral hearing, and the party at fault is at risk as to costs [3].
- **Documents/information required (where sought on documents)**
  - The parties must provide: the documents (including the case management bundle with information sheets fully completed), a draft Order and draft List of Common Ground and Issues (agreed), and statements signed by each advocate confirming specified matters (including NDR steps/plans or why NDR isn’t appropriate), and giving a time estimate for trial (including reading time) [3].
- **What the judge does at the CMC / typical directions**
  - The judge discusses issues and approves the **List of Common Ground and Issues**, discusses requirements (including disclosure), fixes the pre-trial timetable (or as much as practicable), and gives a direction for trial date to be fixed promptly (and sets a trial time estimate) [9].
  - The judge also considers proposals for **IT use**, **document translation**, and may make an **NDR order**; in appropriate cases considers retention/transfer out of the Commercial Court and suitability for schemes; expects to be informed about other similar cases to consider coordinated case management [9].
- **Case management information sheet / bundle deadlines**
  - All parties attending must complete a case management information sheet [6].
  - Each party must provide its completed information sheet to the court (and copy all other parties) **at least 7 days** before the CMC; no separate application notice is necessary for items not covered by the standard questions if written evidence won’t be involved, provided they are entered on the information sheet [6].
  - The case management bundle must be provided to the court **at least 7 days** before the CMC [7].
- **Preliminary issues / summary determination**
  - At the CMC, the court actively considers whether the trial or summary determination of preliminary issue(s) is possible to shorten proceedings, often with reference to Part 24; the court will rarely make an order without at least one party’s concurrence [8].

## Multi-track general rules (CPR Part 29)
- For multi-track cases, the court may set directions and either **fix a CMC and/or pre-trial review**, or give directions and set a timetable between directions and trial [13].
- When giving directions, the court must consider whether to order or encourage **alternative dispute resolution** [13].
- **Who attends**: if a party has a legal representative, the representative must attend, being familiar with the case and having sufficient authority [14].
- **Agreed proposals**: parties must endeavour to agree directions and submit agreed directions (or their proposals) **at least 7 days before** any CMC; if the court approves agreed directions or issues its own directions, the CMC is vacated [15].

### Note / next step
These sources include **Commercial Court**-specific detail and also **general multi-track (CPR Part 29)** rules. If you tell me which court (e.g., Commercial Court vs another multi-track court), I can focus only on the relevant set.

question: How does the Commercial Court handle case management conferences?
answer:
In the Commercial Court, case management conferences (CMCs) are handled as follows:

- **Mandatory CMC and when it should be fixed**: A mandatory CMC should be fixed to be heard **as promptly as possible** while allowing time for necessary preparatory steps, particularly on **disclosure** [3].  
- **Deadlines to fix the CMC (claim start / transfer)**:  
  - If started by **Part 7 claim form**, the **claimant** must take steps to fix the CMC with the **Listing Office** within **14 days** after all defendants who will file and serve a defence have done so [3].  
  - If started by **Part 8 claim form**, the claimant must take steps to fix the CMC within **14 days** after all defendants who wish to serve evidence have done so [3].  
  - If transferred to the Commercial Court, the claimant must apply for a CMC within **14 days** of the **transfer order**, unless the judge already held/gave directions for a CMC in that order [3].  
- **If the claimant doesn’t apply**: If the claimant fails to make the required application, **any other party may apply** for a CMC [4].  
- **Oral hearing vs “documents” CMC**:  
  - Where **all proposed directions are not agreed**, the general rule is that there must be an **oral hearing** [7].  
  - It may be possible to dispense with an oral hearing even where not all directions are agreed **if the issues are straightforward and oral hearing costs can’t be justified** [7].  
  - If a documents CMC is sought, the parties must provide the appropriate documents by **12 noon on the Tuesday** of the week the CMC is fixed for the **Friday**; timing is **strictly enforced** and failure means the CMC should be expected to proceed as an oral hearing [7].  
- **What happens at the CMC (judge’s role)**: The judge will (as necessary) **discuss the issues** (by reference to the draft/final List of Common Ground and Issues), **discuss requirements including disclosure**, and **fix the pre-trial timetable** (or as much as practicable) [9]. The judge will also give directions including (notably) **setting a trial date** (promptly after the hearing unless good reason to defer), consider proposals for **IT**, consider **document translation** where significant, make **NDR** orders in appropriate cases, consider retention/transfer within the Commercial Court and scheme suitability, and expect to be informed about other similar cases [9].  
- **At the first/early CMC, disclosure is reviewed and approved**: At the first CMC the Court will **review and approve, amend or reject** the parties’ proposals for **disclosure** [11].  
- **Consent order where all directions agreed**: Where all proposed directions have been agreed, parties are to file a **proposed Consent Order** as soon as possible, with an agreed covering letter explaining any reasons attendance should not be required [7].  

**Note:** The sources you provided also reference that the Commercial Court case management is governed by **rule 58.13 and PD58 §10** [11].

question: What are the CMC deadlines and procedures?
answer:
## Patents Court CMC (case management conference): deadline and basic procedure

- **Deadline to apply for a CMC (claimant):** the claimant should apply **within 14 days** of the date when **all defendants who intend to file and serve a defence have done so** [1].
- **If the claimant does not apply:** **any other party** may apply for a CMC (under **PD63.5.6**) [1].
- **Early application:** **any party** may apply **in writing** for a CMC **prior to the above periods** [1].
- **If the case is transferred:** the claimant must file for a CMC **within 14 days of the transfer** [1].

## How CMCs are conducted
- **Judge-led (usual):** “almost invariably” Patents Court CMCs are conducted by a **judge** [2].
- **Master-led (limited circumstances):** a **Master may** conduct a CMC only in the limited circumstances set out in **PD63.5.2(2)** [2].
- **Bundles:** bundles “in accordance with **PD63.5.9** should be filed with the court” [2].

## Notes on trial timing (not CMC, but related court process)
- The Patents Court aims to bring patent cases on for trial **within 12 months** of the claim being issued [3].
- Parties are expected to start considering/agreeing trial dates soon after service [3].

question: What is the standard disclosure process?
answer:
**Court-specific note:** The sources provided are **court guides** (King’s Bench, Commercial, Patents). They do not, by themselves, establish the general CPR position for all cases. They explain how each court applies **CPR Part 31** in practice. For the underlying general rules, you should also check the CPR/Practice Direction text itself.

## Standard disclosure process (as described in the guides)

### 1) Two-stage process: list first, then inspection
- Disclosure and inspection of documents involves **two stages**:  
  1) disclosure of the **existence** of documents (and **claiming privilege** from inspection where relevant) **done by list**, and  
  2) **inspection**, where the other side is offered facilities to **inspect** documents. [4]

### 2) Duty triggered by a disclosure order; standard disclosure via Form N265
- After a **disclosure order** is made, a party is under a **duty to disclose**. [5]  
- Parties should give **standard disclosure** by completing **form N265**. [5]

### 3) Content/format of the standard disclosure list and statement (Commercial Court guidance)
Where standard disclosure is used (i.e., where PD 57AD does not apply), the Commercial Court guidance indicates:
- Documents may need to be listed (e.g., in **date order**), **numbered consecutively**, given a **concise description**, and/or use a **Bates number** system. [3]
- If there are many documents in one category, the disclosing party may list them as a **category** unless otherwise ordered. [3]
- **Each party** must serve a **separate list of documents**. [3]
- The **disclosure statement** for standard disclosure should begin with specified “reasonable and proportionate search” wording. [3]
- The disclosure statement for standard disclosure should end with a specified **certificate** confirming understanding of the duty and that the list is complete (to the best of the party’s knowledge). [3]
- An adapted version of **N265(CC)** (standard disclosure list form) is approved for use in the Commercial Court. [3]
- The Commercial Court may order that the disclosure statement be **verified by affidavit** at any stage. [3]

### 4) Inspection linked to what is in the statements
- Parties are required to give **inspection** of any document they refer to in their **statement of case** or in a **witness statement** (and cannot rely on documents they failed to disclose). [5]

### 5) How disclosure is sourced in the Patents Court
- In the Patents Court, parties are obliged to provide disclosure **in accordance with Part 31**, as modified (including the disclosure pilot / related provisions referenced in the guidance). [1][2]

---

question: What is the standard disclosure process?
filter: Civil Procedure Rules and Practice Directions
answer:
The **standard disclosure** process under **CPR Part 31** and **PD 31A** is:

- **Scope:** CPR Part 31 sets rules on disclosure/inspection and applies to all claims **except small claims**. [1]  
- **Meaning of disclosure:** A party discloses a document by **stating it exists (or has existed)**. [2]  
- **Right to inspect:** The receiving party can **inspect disclosed documents**, unless exceptions apply (e.g., the document is no longer in the disclosing party’s control; or a right/duty to withhold applies). [3]  
- **Reasonable search (PD 31A):** To give standard disclosure, the disclosing party must make a **reasonable search** for documents falling within the relevant disclosure categories. [5]  
- **Disclosure list (PD 31A):** After the search, the disclosing party must make a **list** of documents:
  - whose existence the party is aware of,  
  - that fall within the relevant categories, and  
  - that are or have been in the party’s **control** (unless an exception applies). [6]  
- **Form of list:** The list should be in **Form N265**. [8]  
- **Limit/dispense with standard disclosure:** The obligations under standard disclosure may be **dispensed with or limited** by the court or by **written agreement** between the parties (agreement should be lodged with the court). [7]  
- **What counts as a “document” (CPR 31.4):** “Document” includes anything recording information (and therefore covers electronic material too, as reflected in PD 31A’s electronic disclosure provisions). [4][7]  

**Note (missing detail):** The sources you provided reference “standard disclosure” being set out in **CPR 31.6**, but they don’t include the text of **CPR 31.6 itself**, so the actual disclosure categories/content of the standard disclosure order are not shown here. [3]  

**Recommendation:** Check **CPR 31.6 (standard disclosure)** for the categories/contents that drive the reasonable search and list.

## What CPR 31.16 is used for
- A person intending to make a claim may need documents held by a likely defendant, and **if not disclosed voluntarily** (e.g. under pre-action protocols), **CPR 31.16 provides for an application for disclosure before proceedings have started**. [6]
- Where such an application is made and a claim is later issued, the claim will have a different case number, but the court should be told and the two cases will be linked on CE file. [6]

## How it is handled (Chancery Division guidance)
- An order for disclosure before proceedings have started is made **in accordance with CPR 31.16** (Chancery guide says this is in **Section II of CPR PD 57AD**). [2][3]
- The application process (Chancery guidance):
  - **Applications under CPR 31.16** are made by **application notice (N244)**. [4]
  - They are **heard by a Master** unless exceptionally the weight/complexity warrants it being dealt with by a **HCJ**. [4]
  - The application must be supported by a **witness statement**. [5]
  - The **scope of disclosure** should be carefully described and **no wider than strictly necessary**. [5]

## Practical detail (Commercial Court guidance on electronic track data)
- In collision claims involving electronic track data, the Commercial Court guidance expects that, in pre-action correspondence, parties will generally:
  - disclose electronic track data in their control; and
  - provide copies or permit inspection during pre-action correspondence. [1]
- A failure to do so (when requested prior to proceedings) without good reason is **likely to attract a costs sanction**. [1]
- An application under **rule 31.16** for disclosure/inspection of electronic track data before proceedings starts is **likely to be considered favourably** by the Court. [1]

## General (multi-track) case management conferences (CPR Part 29)
- When a case is allocated to the multi-track, the court will give case management directions and a timetable for steps to trial, and **may** fix a **case management conference** and/or a **pre-trial review**, or both, and give other management directions as it sees fit. [6]
- A **case management conference** (or **pre-trial review**) may be fixed **at any time after allocation**. [7]
- If a party has a legal representative, the representative attending must be **familiar with the case** and have **sufficient authority** to deal with issues likely to arise. [7]
- The parties must **try to agree directions** and submit either agreed directions, or their proposals, to the court **at least 7 days before** any case management conference. [8]
- If the court approves agreed directions (or issues its own), the parties will be notified and the **case management conference will be vacated**. [8]

## Practice Direction 29 (scope)
- PD29 applies to claims begun by claim form issued in the **Central Office or Chancery Chambers in the Royal Courts of Justice**. [2]
